entry: Maritime republic centered on Venice, northeastern [[Italy]] (697–1797). Founded, according to tradition, in 697, it grew over about 1,100 years into one of Europe's major commercial and naval powers, annexing much of northeastern Italy, Istria, Dalmatia and numerous Adriatic and eastern Ionian islands. Between the 13th and 16th centuries it also governed [[Crete]], [[Cyprus]], the Peloponnese and several Greek islands. In 1509 a coalition of the [[Habsburg monarchy]], Spain and France defeated Venice at the Battle of Agnadello, though it kept most of its mainland possessions. Wars with the [[Ottoman Empire]] ended with the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718, after which Venice had lost all its Aegean possessions. Occupied by [[Napoleon]]'s French troops in 1797, the republic was divided with the Habsburg monarchy under the Treaty of Campo Formio. Its head of state, the doge, was elective from the late 9th century, and its administration was directed by the Great Council, Senate and Council of Ten.

Country on the western coast of Central Africa, west of the [[Congo River]]. It is bordered by [[Gabon]], [[Cameroon]], the [[Central African Republic]], the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] and the Angolan exclave of Cabinda. Bantu-speaking peoples dominated the region at least 3,000 years ago. [[France]] colonized the area in the late 19th century, incorporating it into French Equatorial Africa. The republic was established on November 28, 1958, and gained independence from France in 1960. From 1969 to 1992 it was a Marxist–Leninist state called the People's Republic of the Congo. After multiparty elections in 1992, the elected government was overthrown in a civil war, and Denis Sassou Nguesso, president from 1979 to 1992, returned to office in 1997 and has remained president since. It is the fourth-largest oil producer in the Gulf of Guinea, and its economy depends on oil, with growth slowing after the post-2015 drop in oil prices.

U.S. political party, founded in 1854 and known as the Grand Old Party (GOP). Its anti-slavery founders opposed the Kansas–Nebraska Act, and the party became the main rival of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]]. [[Abraham Lincoln]]'s 1860 election led to Southern secession and the [[American Civil War]], and the party led efforts to preserve the Union and abolish slavery. [[Ronald Reagan]]'s 1980 election realigned national politics. Since 2009 a shift toward right-wing populism culminated in the 2016 election of [[Donald Trump]]. The party favors tariffs, opposes free trade and labor unions, and broadly opposes abortion, LGBT rights, immigration and gun control.

One of two political entities of [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], in the country's north and east. Established in 1992 at the start of the [[Bosnian War]] to safeguard the interests of Bosnia's Serbs, it was made one of the country's two constituent entities by the 1995 Dayton Agreement. Its administrative center and largest city is Banja Luka. It recorded a population of 1,228,423 in the 2013 census and has a National Assembly of 83 seats. Its powers resemble those of a sovereign state in many respects, and most of the country's Serb population lives within it.

Enlarged [[Lake|lake]] behind a [[Dam|dam]], usually built to store fresh water and often doubling for hydroelectric power generation. Reservoirs can be created by controlling a watercourse that drains an existing body of water, by interrupting a watercourse to form an embayment, by excavation, or by building retaining walls or [[Levee|levees]] around an area. Dammed reservoirs flood a valley, with the dam built at its narrowest practical point. On-stream reservoirs lie on the original streambed and are filled by creeks, rivers or runoff, while off-stream reservoirs receive water diverted through an [[Aqueduct (water supply)|aqueduct]] or [[Pipeline|pipeline]]. Bank-side reservoirs store water [[Siphon|siphoned]] or pumped from rivers of variable quality, enclosed by embankments that may exceed 6 km (4 miles) in circumference. Water may stay in them for several months, during which biological processes can substantially reduce many contaminants. London's water supply draws from the [[River Thames]] and River Lea into such storage.

Japanese horror game series and media franchise created by Capcom, known as Biohazard in Japan. The first game, released for the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] in 1996, is credited with defining the survival horror genre and returning [[Zombie|zombies]] to popular culture. [[Resident Evil 4]] (2005) shifted the series toward over-the-shoulder action. The live-action film series began in 2002 with *Resident Evil*, and a [[Netflix]] series aired in 2022. With over 218 million video game copies sold as of October 2026, the franchise is Capcom's best-selling and the best-selling horror game franchise. Its films have grossed more than $1.6 billion.

Survival horror game for the [[GameCube]], developed and published by Capcom in 2005. Players control special agent Leon S. Kennedy on a mission to rescue the U.S. president's daughter, Ashley Graham, who has been abducted by a religious [[Cult|cult]] in rural [[Spain]]. The game departed from the fixed camera angles and slower play of earlier [[Resident Evil]] games, using a dynamic camera and action-horror gameplay. It was part of the Capcom Five, a set of GameCube exclusives, and won multiple Game of the Year awards. It sold 15.2 million copies by March 2025. A remake was released in 2023.

Highly viscous liquid or solid, typically harvested from plants, that can be converted into a [[Polymer|polymer]]. Resins are mixtures of organic compounds insoluble in water, predominantly terpenes. Plant resins protect against insects and pathogens and are secreted in response to injury. Common examples include pine oleoresins, [[Amber|amber]], hashish, frankincense, myrrh and shellac, an animal-derived resin. Amber is [[Fossil|fossil]] resin from coniferous and other trees, while subfossil copal becomes tacky when a drop of [[Acetone]] or [[Chloroform]] is placed on it. Resins are used in varnishes, [[Adhesive|adhesives]], [[Incense|incenses]] and [[Perfume|perfumes]].

Passive two-terminal electronic component that provides electrical resistance in a circuit. Resistors reduce [[Electric current|current]] flow, adjust signal levels, divide [[Voltage|voltages]], bias active elements and terminate transmission lines. High-power types dissipate many [[Watt|watts]] as heat in motor controls, power distribution systems or test loads for generators. Variable resistors serve as volume controls or lamp dimmers, or as sensors of heat, light, humidity, force or chemical activity. Resistors are ubiquitous in electronic equipment and are also implemented within [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]]. Their function is set by resistance, measured in [[Ohm|ohms]], and commercial resistors span more than nine orders of magnitude. Under [[Ohm's law]], the voltage across a resistor is proportional to the current through it, with its resistance as the constant of proportionality.

Phenomenon in which an oscillating system absorbs energy at its [[Frequency|resonant frequency]] and responds with maximum amplitude. It occurs when an external force or vibration matches that frequency, and the system then vibrates with greater [[Amplitude|amplitude]] than at other frequencies. This can be useful, as in musical instruments or radio receivers, but it can also cause excessive vibration or structural failure. Resonance occurs in mechanical, electrical, acoustic and electromagnetic systems, as well as in nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and electron spin resonance (ESR). Resonant systems can generate a specific frequency, as in musical instruments, or select one from a complex vibration, as in filters. The term comes from [[Latin]] *resonantia*, "echo", and originated in acoustics, where [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] discussed sympathetic resonance in musical instruments in *Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences*.

Positive [[Feeling|feeling]] or deferential action toward someone or something considered important, also called esteem. Respect conveys admiration for good or valuable qualities, and it can also mean honoring someone by showing care and consideration for their needs or feelings. In many [[Culture|cultures]], people are considered worthy of respect until they prove otherwise. In honor cultures, respect is more often earned through exemplary actions or social roles than granted by default. Courtesies vary: they may be words such as "thank you" in the West or *namaste* in the [[Indian subcontinent]], or physical signs such as a slight bow, a smile, direct eye contact or a handshake. Such acts can carry very different meanings depending on cultural context.

Biological process of transporting oxygen from the environment to body tissues and removing carbon dioxide, using a respiratory system. Gas exchange in the lungs occurs through [[Breathing|ventilation]] (commonly called breathing), the movement of air in and out of the lungs, and perfusion, the pulmonary circulation of [[Blood|blood]] through the [[Capillary|pulmonary capillaries]]. Inhalation is usually active, while exhalation is usually passive, though speaking, singing, coughing and swimming involve active exhalation. Each breath of about 350 mL does not fill the alveoli with fresh air; it is mixed with about 2.5 L of functional residual capacity, the gas that remains in the lungs after each exhalation. Mechanisms keep this gas composition constant as it equilibrates with the blood. Physiological respiration differs from [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]], the metabolic process by which cells obtain energy from nutrients in the form of ATP and NADPH. Cellular respiration produces [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and water as waste products.

Condition in which inadequate gas exchange leaves arterial oxygen, [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]], or both outside normal levels. A drop in blood oxygen is called hypoxemia, and a rise in arterial carbon dioxide is called hypercapnia. Respiratory failure is classified as Type 1 or Type 2, depending on whether carbon dioxide is high, and it can be acute or chronic. Clinical trials usually define it by increased respiratory rate, abnormal blood gases, or evidence of increased work of breathing. It can cause an altered state of consciousness because of ischemia in the brain. Typical reference values are PaO₂ above 80 mmHg (11 kPa) and PaCO₂ below 45 mmHg (6.0 kPa).

Negative-sense, single-stranded [[RNA]] virus that causes infections of the respiratory tract. It is a common cause of respiratory hospitalization in infants, and reinfection is common later in life, usually with less severity. Infections can cause bronchiolitis in infants, [[Common cold|colds]] in adults, and [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]] in older people and those who are immunocompromised. Infection rates are typically higher during cold winter months. In May 2023 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first RSV vaccines. Severe illness is treated mainly with supportive care such as oxygen, and the antiviral ribavirin is licensed for treating RSV in children.

Small [[Trogon|trogon]] of tropical montane forests in [[Central America]] and southern [[Mexico]]. The species, *Pharomachrus mocinno*, has two recognized subspecies. It is mostly omnivorous, eating mainly the fruits of the laurel family (Lauraceae) and occasionally insects, [[Lizard|lizards]], frogs and snails. Males have iridescent green plumes, a red lower breast and belly, black innerwings and a white undertail, while females are duller, with a shorter tail. Nests are made in holes in decaying trees, often ones made by [[Woodpecker|woodpeckers]]. The female usually lays one to three eggs, which hatch in 17 to 19 days. The species is near threatened on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, mainly because of habitat destruction. It is the national animal of [[Guatemala]], shown on its flag and coat of arms, and it gives its name to the Guatemalan quetzal currency.

Business that prepares and serves [[Food|food]] and beverages to customers. Meals are generally eaten on the premises, but many restaurants also offer take-out and delivery. Establishments range from inexpensive [[Fast food|fast-food]] outlets and cafeterias to mid-priced family restaurants and high-priced luxury venues. Early precursors include a site in Mesopotamia dated to about 2700 BCE, with benches, an oven and numerous standardized bowls, which researchers interpret as a communal dining space. An Egyptian record from 512 BC mentions a public [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptian]] eating establishment that served only one dish. In [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]] and [[Ancient Rome|Rome]], the *thermopolium* sold ready-to-eat food and drink, and [[Pompeii]] has yielded 158 such establishments with service counters. These were most often frequented by people who lacked private kitchens.

Concept of coming back to life after death. It differs from [[Reincarnation|reincarnation]], which involves returning in a different body. The English word derives from Latin *resurrectio*, from *surgere*, "to rise". Egyptian and Canaanite religions had cults of dying-and-rising gods such as [[Osiris]] and Baal. In the [[Hebrew Bible]], resurrection is rare, confined to a few prophetic miracles and to Daniel. Bodily resurrection was affirmed in 2 Maccabees, accepted by the Pharisees and rejected by the Sadducees, and was later fixed by [[Maimonides]] among the Thirteen Principles of Faith. In the Abrahamic religions, a universal resurrection at the end of the world is a standard belief, and early Christianity made the resurrection of [[Jesus]] its central doctrine. The Apostles' Creed and the [[Nicene Creed]] codify belief in a general resurrection and judgment. Hinduism and [[Buddhism]] center on rebirth rather than resurrection, though both preserve stories of the dead restored to life. Cryonics, which is widely regarded as [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]], is a speculative technology, and the resurrection of long-dead bodies is not considered possible with current science.

Non-venomous python, *Malayopython reticulatus*, native to South and [[Southeast Asia]]. The mainland subspecies is the world's longest snake. It is a constrictor and an excellent swimmer that has colonized many small islands. Because of its wide range, it is listed as least concern on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. It is hunted for its skin, for [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]] and for the [[Pet|pet]] trade, making it one of the most economically important reptiles. Humans, including adults, have occasionally been killed, sometimes swallowed wholly or partly, most recently in [[Indonesia]], especially on Sulawesi and nearby islands.

Withdrawal from one's position or occupation, or from active working life. Many people retire when elderly or unable to work for health reasons, or when they become eligible for [[Pension|pension]] benefits, while others are forced out by illness, accident or legislation. Some semi-retire by reducing hours or workload. Retirement is a recent idea in most countries, introduced in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Before then, low [[Life expectancy|life expectancy]], lack of social security and the absence of pensions meant most workers continued until death. Germany was the first country to introduce retirement benefits, in 1889, under [[Otto von Bismarck]]. As of March 2023, only about 15% of U.S. private-industry workers had access to a traditional defined-benefit pension plan, while about 75% of public-sector workers participated in pension plans. In many poorer countries, older people rely on family support.

British news agency wholly owned by Thomson Reuters, a multinational [[Conglomerate (company)|information conglomerate]]. It was established in [[London]] in 1851 by the German-born British baron Paul Reuter. Reuters employs about 2,500 journalists and 600 photojournalists in 200 locations in 165 countries, writing in 16 languages. It has no single headquarters, and its leadership is split between New York and London. The Thomson Corporation of Canada acquired it in a 2008 merger. In December 2024 Reuters was ranked the 27th most visited news site in the world, with over 105 million monthly readers.

Harmful act against a person or group in response to a real or perceived grievance. Vengeful forms of [[Justice|justice]], such as primitive or retributive justice, are often distinguished from formal forms such as distributive or restorative justice. In societies that value [[Honour|honor]], an injury can upset a "balance of honor", prompting family members to retaliate, and the cycle may spread to a whole community and last for generations. Feuds, cycles of provocation and retaliation carried out by families or tribal groups, were important in many pre-industrial societies, especially around the Mediterranean. They persist in [[Albania]], where *gjakmarrja* (blood feuds) can involve an offender's extended relations, and in Kurdish regions of [[Turkey]] and in [[Papua New Guinea]]. In Japan, *katakiuchi*, revenge killings to honor one's family, clan or lord, is now most often pursued by peaceful means. [[Francis Bacon]] called revenge "wild justice".

Water purification process using a semi-permeable membrane. Pressure is applied to overcome [[Osmosis|osmotic]] pressure, so that water passes through the membrane while dissolved substances are retained on the pressurized side. The process can remove dissolved or suspended chemical species as well as biological matter, principally [[Bacteria|bacteria]], and is used in industry and to produce potable water. It is best known for [[Desalination|desalination]] of seawater, removing salt and other materials from the water. As of 2013 the world's largest reverse osmosis desalination plant was in Sorek, Israel, producing 624 thousand cubic meters per day.

Abstract strategy [[Board game|board game]] for two players, played on an 8×8 uncheckered board. It was invented in 1883. Each player uses 64 identical disks, light on one side and dark on the other, and chooses one color for the game. Players take turns placing disks on empty squares. Opposing disks lying in a straight line between the new disk and another disk of the mover's color are turned over. When all playable squares are filled, the player with more disks showing their color wins. [[Othello]], a variant with a fixed initial setup, was patented in 1971.

Rapid, fundamental transformation of a society's class, state, ethnic or religious structures. According to the sociologist Jack Goldstone, revolutions share a core of efforts to change the political regime through a competing vision of a just order, notable mass mobilization, and noninstitutionalized action such as demonstrations, strikes or violence. Some begin with peasant uprisings or guerrilla warfare on a country's periphery; others with urban insurrection aimed at seizing the capital. They may be inspired by ideologies such as nationalism, republicanism, [[Democracy|democracy]], liberalism, [[Fascism|fascism]] or [[Socialism|socialism]]. A regime may become vulnerable after military defeat, economic chaos, or persistent repression and corruption. Revolutions typically provoke counter-revolutions, and autocracies that take power during them tend to be durable. Notable examples include the [[American Revolution]] (1765–1783), the [[French Revolution]] (1789–1799), the [[Haitian Revolution]] (1791–1804), the [[Mexican Revolution]] (1910–1920) and the [[Iranian Revolution]] of 1979.

Series of revolutions across Europe between January 1848 and October 1849, also known as the springtime of the peoples. More than fifty countries were affected, though revolutionaries coordinated little. They generally opposed conservative systems such as [[Absolute monarchy|absolute monarchy]] and [[Feudalism|feudalism]], and sought nation states founded on constitutionalism and popular sovereignty. The wave began in [[Sicily]] in January 1848 and spread after the revolution in France in February. Causes included dissatisfaction with political leadership, demands for democracy and a free press, working-class demands for economic rights, and rising [[Nationalism|nationalism]]. The European potato failure caused mass starvation, migration and unrest. Many revolutions were quickly suppressed, with tens of thousands killed and many more exiled. Still, reforms included the abolition of [[Serfdom|serfdom]] in [[Austrian Empire|Austria]] and Hungary, the end of absolute monarchy in [[Denmark]], and representative democracy in the [[Netherlands]].
